newsitem.title: USA: U.S. in new 'open skies' efforts in Asia.
newsitem.headline: U.S. in new 'open skies' efforts in Asia.

text.p: A senior U.S. Transportation Department official said on Thursday the United States next year would put new emphasis on reaching "open skies" accords in the many closed aviation markets of Asia.
"I look forward to good news on this front in a period of months ... rather than years," Mark Gerchick, deputy assistant secretary for aviation and international affairs, said.

He told the North American section of the Airports Council International, an airports trade group, that after recent successes in Europe, efforts would now go to write accords with smaller Asian nations. Japan was the prize, he said.

The open markets reached with smaller European countries led to the "open skies" pact with Germany, officials say, and played a role in talks underway with Britain and wider discussions with the European Union.
He said efforts to remove aviation restrictions were also underway with France and Portugal.

He made no comment on the progress of the British talks but he restated the U.S. position that nothing short of a full free market accord, with the opening of London's Heathrow airport to additional American flights, would be acceptable.
Gerchick said Asia is the world's fastest-growing aviation market, and Japan is the key, but Washington has not yet been able to negotiate an "open skies" pact with Tokyo.
He said the United States wanted an Asia-wide consensus on openness "until 'open skies' becomes a guiding intellectual paradigm in Asia just as it is fast becoming in Europe."

Gerchick said talks were underway with Malaysia, Taiwan, South Korea, Singapore and New Zealand and was optimistic of getting results to form the critical mass needed to persaude bigger nations drop their aviation barriers.

He said a study showed that Japan was greatly underserved by international air services and that new routes have a major impact on domestic growth. And, he said, three new airlines have recently started up in Japan to fill the void.
"This is bound to have an impact on the thinking of regulators in Japan," Gerchick said.
Answering questions, he said the administration was looking into easing the law limiting foreign ownership of U.S. airlines to 25 percent, but did not indicate its thinking.
Congress has long opposed relaxing the limitation.
